title: Cockney Rhyming Slang: Beautiful Gibberish
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Cockney rhyming slang, the London working-class slang where a two-word phrase stands in for a word, with the second word rhyming with the target (e.g., apples and pears for stairs, Barney Rubble for trouble). They cover how the second word is often dropped, examples like dog and bone for phone, bread and honey for money, Todd Sloan for alone, and Aristotle for ass, plus exceptions like raspberry tart for fart. The hosts discuss origins: the criminal-code theory, the argument by Dick Sullivan that street cops would have known it, John Camden Hotten's attribution to shaunters and patterers (street hawkers) around Seven Dials, and Victorian back slang. They touch on Cockney identity, its spread to Australia and the US West Coast, pop culture uses (Guy Ritchie films, Not on Your Nellie, The Sweeney), newer rhyming terms, and why it has lasted. The episode ends with a listener email about a 2000 encounter with a police officer during the Satanic panic, tied to a rerun-style Saturday Select of the Satanic Panic episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and Seattle show promo
segments.summary: Josh promotes a Seattle live show and the hosts chat about The Limey, Guy Ritchie films, and their first exposure to Cockney rhyming slang.

segments.title: What Cockney rhyming slang is
segments.summary: The hosts define the structure: a two-word phrase whose second word rhymes with the intended word, often unrelated in meaning, and often with the second word dropped later.

segments.title: Examples: apples and pears, Barney Rubble, bread and honey
segments.summary: Examples include Barney Rubble for trouble, apples and pears for stairs (later shortened to apples), bread and honey for money (shortened to bread), and dog and bone for phone.

segments.title: Undocumented usage, twist, Todd Sloan and raspberry tart
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how slang is rarely written down, the word twist from twist and twirl, on your Todd from jockey Todd Sloan's memoir line, and blowing a raspberry from raspberry tart.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a brief transition back to the show.

segments.title: Put up your dukes, Aristotle for ass, and rhyming dictionaries
segments.summary: The hosts discuss put up your dukes, the ass slang chain from bottle and glass to Aristotle to aris to ours, and the existence of rhyming dictionaries.

segments.title: Origins: criminals, Dick Sullivan, Hotten, shaunters and patterers
segments.summary: The criminal code theory is questioned because street cops came from the same neighborhoods. John Camden Hotten attributes it to shaunters and patterers, street sellers around Seven Dials. Victorian back slang and Irish stock worker theories are also discussed and doubted.

segments.title: Cockney identity, spread, pop culture, and staying power
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Cockney as a working-class identity, its spread to Australia and the US West Coast, TV shows The Sweeney and Not on Your Nellie, and why the slang has lasted, including new rhymes and a Museum of London survey.

segments.title: Satanic Panic rerun and listener email
segments.summary: Josh introduces a re-released Saturday Select of the Satanic Panic episode and reads a listener email about a 2000 encounter with a police officer who searched a teen's bedroom.
